metadata.title: Transformers in SERS-ML: What the Rewrite Actually Fixed
metadata.note: Compares the initial draft of Section 4.2 (Transformer Architectures) against the revised version, covering three real changes: the addition of a closing recommendation, the qualification of an unqualified accuracy claim, and the resolution of an evidence gap through a real peer-reviewed benchmark.

beats.narration_text: This is Liam, in for Kumar Karthik. Section 4.2, on transformer architectures, went through a real revision, not a polish pass. Comparing the very first draft against what's there now shows three actual changes: a missing recommendation, an unqualified accuracy claim, and an evidence gap that used to just sit there unaddressed. Walk me through what changed and why.

props.segment: Transformers in SERS-ML: What the Rewrite Actually Fixed
props.command: Compare the first draft of section 4.2 against the current version and explain what actually changed and why.
output: an unqualified '100%' claim got real context
a real evidence gap finally got closed

beats.narration_text: The first draft of this section read complete. It covered three transformer studies in full detail, methods, results, deployment concerns, all laid out clearly. But covering studies in detail isn't the same as judging them. There was no recommendation, an unqualified accuracy claim standing without context, and a real comparison gap the draft only pointed at instead of actually closing. That gap between describing evidence and building an argument from it is the actual difference between a first draft and a finished one.

props.text:
4.2 was complete.
Wait, descriptive.
No recommendation.
Now it's honest.

beats.narration_text: The original text summarized three transformer studies, Wang et al., Zhang et al., Hajikhani et al., and then just stopped. No verdict on when any of this is actually worth using. That's the exact gap the paper's own guidelines are built to catch: describing evidence isn't the same as recommending something from it. The rewrite closes that gap directly. Default to a CNN for most SERS classification work, and reach for a transformer only when the problem genuinely needs multi-task output or long-range spectral dependencies.

beats.narration_text: The original draft stated that Wang et al.'s transformer network achieved a 100% identification rate, full stop, with no context on what that actually meant. Going back to the source paper found the real testing conditions: a validation set of just 75 spectra, collected under only two laser power levels and a narrow range of integration times. Adding that detail changes what the number means, a hundred percent on a small, narrow test isn't evidence the method generalizes. It's a strong result on a controlled trial, and the rewrite says so plainly.

production_viz.mechanic: a large percentage figure annotated with its actual test conditions
production_viz.note: real conditions from the source paper (75 spectra, two laser power levels, narrow integration range), no invented numbers

beats.narration_text: Here's what the original draft never addressed at all. Three separate transformer studies get cited in this one section, Wang et al., Zhang et al., Hajikhani et al., and not one of them is ever benchmarked directly against a CNN on the same data. Without that comparison, there's no real way to know whether the transformer architecture itself is doing the work, or whether a well-tuned CNN would perform just as well on the same task.

a box labeled 'CNN' grows in on the right

production_viz.label: no direct transformer-vs-CNN comparison exists in the cited studies
production_viz.mechanic: two labeled boxes with a growing question mark between them

beats.narration_text: So the rewrite went and found a real answer instead of just flagging the gap. A 2026 peer-reviewed study by Sineesh and Kamsali directly compared five deep learning architectures, transformer included, on the same Raman classification task under one unified protocol. The transformer finished last, more than five points behind the best model. It's worth being honest about the limits here: this benchmark used general Raman data, not SERS specifically. But it's real, independent evidence that a transformer doesn't automatically win, and that's exactly what the section's final recommendation is now built on.

production_viz.label: the real benchmark that closed the comparison gap
production_viz.mechanic: five-bar comparison, transformer finishing last, with citation and scope caveat
production_viz.note: real citation (Sineesh & Kamsali, 2026), explicitly scoped as general Raman not SERS-specific, no invented numbers beyond what's reported

beats.narration_text: So: the original draft summarized three transformer studies and offered no recommendation, the rewrite adds one. An unqualified hundred percent claim now carries the actual conditions it was measured under, seventy-five spectra, two laser power levels. And a comparison the section used to just gesture at got closed with a real, independent benchmark showing the transformer finishing last among five architectures tested. That's the actual difference between describing a literature and building an argument out of it.

artifactLines: The original draft summarized three transformer studies with no closing recommendation.
The rewrite adds one: default to CNN, use a transformer only for multi-task or long-range needs.
Wang et al.'s unqualified '100%' claim now carries its real test conditions: 75 spectra, two laser power levels.
A comparison the section only gestured at got closed with a real benchmark (Sineesh & Kamsali, 2026).
That benchmark found the transformer finishing last among five architectures tested.
Naming a gap and actually closing it are two different things — this rewrite did both.
